Glossary of Financial Terms

Contact Information

We offer a list of financial terms and definitions that can help you with certain banking, credit, or loan expressions. Some words or terms, especially those of common legal use, may have different or additional definitions outside this context. All acronyms used in this glossary represent the abbreviations of the corresponding terms in English.

Letter Terms

A

Attorney: A licensed professional authorized to practice law. In some real estate transactions, an attorney may perform functions such as drafting the real estate contract, title search, and closing.

Creditor (or lender): A person, company, or organization that lends money to the debtor. It also refers to the company that issues credit cards.

Asset: Something you own that has value.

Financial Asset: An asset with monetary value, such as the balance in a savings account, cash in your pocket, or money in an investment fund.

Physical Asset: Something you own that has value and can be seen and touched. It has a physical presence. A computer is a physical asset.

Productive Asset: Something you own that has value and can help you produce more assets, often earning more money. Education and training can be productive assets. A lawnmower can also be a productive asset.

Forbearance Agreement: If you meet certain requirements, a forbearance agreement allows you to temporarily stop making payments or temporarily reduce your monthly payment amount for a specified period. For all types of federal student loans, you are responsible for paying the interest that accrues during a forbearance period. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Reasonable Accommodation: In housing, a reasonable accommodation is a change in rules, policies, practices, or services to allow a person with a disability the same opportunity to use and enjoy a housing unit or common space.

Adjudication: When used in the context of insurance claims, adjudication is the process of reviewing claims. The insurance company determines if a loss is covered by your insurance policy. If the loss is covered, the insurance company also decides the amount it will pay and the amount you have to pay.

Late Payment Warning: Explanation of what will happen if you do not make at least the required minimum payment on time.

Credit Reporting Agency: Companies that produce credit reports. They may be called credit reporting agencies, credit bureaus, or credit reporting companies.

Agent: A person authorized to act on behalf of another person or entity, the principal.

Insurance Agent: An insurance agent recommends how much insurance you need and indicates its cost.

Title Insurance Agent: A professional who investigates the property's title to ensure the seller has the right to sell it. The agent also checks what claims lenders or other parties may have on the property.

Real Estate Agent: A professional who can help you find a home and guide you through the buying process.

Save: Set aside a portion of the money you earn or receive to use in the future.

Initial Fraud Alert: If you are concerned that you may be a victim of identity theft or fraud, you can place an initial fraud alert with one of the national credit reporting agencies. A fraud alert can make it harder for an identity thief to open more accounts in your name. When you have an alert on your report, a company must verify your identity before issuing credit, so they may try to contact you. The alert is free and lasts for one year. Once it expires, you can get a new one.

Extended Fraud Alert: A request you can make to a national credit reporting agency that requires potential lenders to verify your identity before granting you credit. The alert is free and lasts for seven years. A copy of an identity theft report is required.

Active Duty Military Alert: A request that active-duty military personnel can make to a national credit reporting agency to help minimize their risk of identity theft. It requires potential lenders to verify the service member's identity. The alert is free and lasts for one year, with the option to renew it for additional one-year periods while the soldier is mobilized.

Amortization: Paying off a loan with periodic payments over a period of time, so the amount you owe decreases with each payment.

Annuity: A contract authorized by an insurance company that guarantees income in exchange for a lump sum or periodic payments.

Mobile Wallet Application: A type of mobile application connected to your account at a financial institution or a credit card, used to make purchases at points of sale. Instead of using a physical debit or credit card, you use the application on your phone.

Employer Contribution: The amount of money an employer contributes to the cost of employee benefits. For example, an employer and an employee might each pay a portion of the cost of health insurance premiums.

Appreciation: An increase in the value of an item over time.

Pre-Approval: A lender's commitment to lend you money under certain conditions they specify.

Housing Counselor: A professional who provides instruction and advice on the home-buying process.

Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF): A federal program that helps families with children who meet the requirements when parents or other responsible relatives cannot meet the family's basic needs.

Rotating Savings and Credit Association (ROSCA): A group of people who meet regularly to contribute money to a savings fund. Each member receives the money from the savings fund according to a schedule. These groups are known by different names worldwide, such as lending circle, tanda, or hui. There may also be other characteristics. The programs are based on trust among group members.

Unincorporated Association: An association of two or more people formed for a religious, educational, charitable, social, or other non-commercial purpose. Unincorporated association accounts constitute a separate category of account ownership, which also includes corporations and partnerships.

Appraisal: A written document that shows an opinion on the value of a home or other asset.

Cash Advance: When you obtain cash using your credit card. You will have to pay it back, probably with interest and fees. Read your credit card agreement to see how a cash advance is defined.

Adverse Action Notice: A notice that lenders must give you if they deny your loan application or take another form of adverse action against you based on your credit reports or credit scores.

Risk-Based Pricing Notice: A notice that lenders must provide if they offer someone less favorable loan terms than other borrowers based on that person's credit reports or scores.

B

Mobile Banking and Online Banking: Access to your account at a financial institution through a mobile application or an Internet browser. It generally allows you to pay bills, deposit checks, and perform other transactions through a mobile application or an Internet browser. You may also be able to communicate electronically with your financial institution.

Bankruptcy: A legal process that allows people who can no longer pay their debts to start over by liquidating assets to pay their debts or creating a payment plan.

Closed Bank: An FDIC-insured bank that has been closed by the supervisory authority (the one that granted its license) and the FDIC has been appointed receiver.

Beneficiary: An eligible beneficiary is a person or entity designated or identified in bank account records or a written trust who will have an interest in the trust upon the account holder's death. To be eligible as a beneficiary, it must be a living person, a charity, or a nonprofit organization. If a charity or nonprofit organization is named as a beneficiary, it must be eligible as such under the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) criteria. Irrevocable trusts often contain additional conditions that must be met before a beneficiary has the right to receive the funds.

Eligible Beneficiary: To be eligible as a beneficiary, it must be a living person, a charity, or a nonprofit organization. If a charity or nonprofit organization is named as a beneficiary, it must be eligible as such under the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) criteria.

Credit Freeze: A product from credit reporting agencies that is similar to a credit freeze. It is not a right provided by law.

Rate Lock or Guaranteed Interest Rate on a Mortgage: The interest rate offered to you on a mortgage will not change during the time it takes to close the home purchase if: You close within the specified period (the rate lock period) and There are no changes to your mortgage application.

U.S. Savings Bond: A low-risk way to save money for the future. By purchasing one, you are lending money to the U.S. government. In return, the U.S. government returns that money, plus interest, to the person in whose name the savings bond is registered. Savings bonds can be purchased for as little as $25.00 through TreasuryDirect.gov. You need to hold a savings bond for at least one year before cashing it. If you cash a savings bond within the first five years of ownership, you will lose three months of interest.

Treasury Bond: A type of non-deposit investment product.

Emergency Financial First Aid Kit (EFFAK): A collection of documents and financial information to keep in a safe place, as advised by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Go to the FEMA website and search for “EFFAK” to download the Emergency Financial First Aid Kit (EFFAK): Strengthen Your Financial Preparedness for Disasters and Emergencies.

Bank Search: A database that allows the user to obtain information about a group of banks (such as all banks with a certain name or location) or about a single FDIC-insured institution by entering increasingly specific search criteria. In addition to confirming a bank's insurance status, the Bank Search system also provides a wide variety of data about each bank, such as: Since when the bank has been insured The name under which the bank is currently insured by the FDIC The location of the bank's main office and branches, by state and address The bank's main website (as reported by the bank to the FDIC) A brief history of the bank, including a list of events by date, such as mergers, branch acquisitions, etc. The bank's operational status—e.g., is it open and operating, or was it closed by its supervisory authority and the FDIC was appointed receiver?

C

Safe Deposit Box: A locked storage provided by some banks to their customers. Since it is not a deposit, the contents of a safe deposit box are not insured by the FDIC.

ATM: Machines that process a variety of banking transactions, including accepting deposits and loan payments, providing cash for withdrawals, and transferring money.

Bank Rating: A rating assigned to a bank by one or more analysts based on the perceived safety and soundness of the bank.

Cashing a Check: Converting a check into cash.

Capacity: Your present and future ability to make your payments. Lenders may use capacity as a factor to determine your creditworthiness.

Capital: The value of your assets and your net worth. Lenders may use this as a factor to determine your creditworthiness.

Capital: The amount of money you borrow and must repay, usually with interest.

Net Capital: The value of an asset minus the liability related to that asset. It is the portion of the asset that you own. For example, if the market value of your home is $100,000 and you still owe $80,000 on the mortgage, your net capital would be $20,000.

Charges: Additional charges in loan and credit contracts, credit cards, and prepaid cards. Charges are not interest. Review the documentation that accompanies these contracts, accounts, or cards to know if charges can be applied and when.

Finance Charge: The dollar amount it will cost you to obtain credit. This is one of the terms used in a disclosure under the Truth in Lending Act (TILA).

Monthly Fee for Prepaid Cards: A fee charged by the provider of a prepaid card each month, even if the prepaid card was not used that month. The fee is automatically deducted from the card balance. Review the documentation that accompanies the card to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Cash Advance Fee: A fee for using a credit card to obtain cash. Review the documentation that accompanies the account to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Balance Inquiry Fee: A fee charged when you check the balance of your deposit account or prepaid card at an ATM, or if you call customer service to inquire about your balance. Review the documentation that accompanies the account or card to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Inactivity Fee for Prepaid Cards: A fee charged by the provider of a prepaid card if the card is not used for a long time. The time period that triggers an inactivity fee varies. Review the documentation that accompanies the card to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Late Payment Fee: Money you have to pay because the creditor did not receive at least the minimum amount due on a debt by the due date.

Bill Payment Fee with Prepaid Cards: A fee charged by the provider of a prepaid card to pay bills online through their website. Review the documentation that accompanies the card to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Account or Card Reload Fee: A fee charged for adding money to a prepaid card. Review the documentation that accompanies the card to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Replacement Fee for Lost or Stolen Prepaid Card: A fee that the provider of your prepaid card may charge to replace your card if it is lost, stolen, or damaged. Review the documentation that accompanies the card to know if this fee can be applied and when.

ATM Withdrawal Fee: A fee charged when you withdraw money at an ATM. Generally, you can use ATMs of your own financial institution without incurring fees. Your institution may also be part of a larger ATM network that does not charge fees. Review the documentation that accompanies the account to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Over-the-Limit Fee: A fee charged for borrowing more money than the creditor agreed to lend you in advance (your credit limit). Review the documentation that accompanies the credit card or other loan to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Additional Card Fee: A fee charged for adding another credit card to your account for use by the person you designate as an authorized user. That card allows the designated authorized user to make credit purchases that you are ultimately responsible for paying. Review the documentation that accompanies the account to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Transaction Fee for Prepaid Cards: A fee that a prepaid card provider charges each time the card is used for certain types of transactions, such as making purchases or loading money onto the card. Review the documentation that accompanies the card to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Foreign Transaction Fee: A fee charged for making purchases in foreign currency with a credit card or prepaid card. It may be called a currency conversion fee. Review the documentation that accompanies the account or card to know if this fee can be applied and when.

Balance Transfer Fee: A fee charged for transferring balances from one credit card or loan to another.

Account Category: A specific form of account ownership as established in the FDIC's deposit insurance regulations. By meeting the requirements of each ownership category, deposits held under that ownership receive separate insurance coverage from the FDIC. The most common ownership categories are: individual accounts; certain retirement accounts; joint accounts; revocable trust accounts; irrevocable trust accounts; employee benefit plans; accounts of corporations, partnerships, and unincorporated associations; and public unit accounts. Also called Ownership Category.

Ownership Category: A specific form of account ownership as established in the FDIC's deposit insurance regulations. By meeting the requirements of each ownership category, deposits held under that ownership receive separate insurance coverage from the FDIC. The most common ownership categories are: individual accounts; certain retirement accounts; joint accounts; revocable trust accounts; irrevocable trust accounts; employee benefit plans; accounts of corporations, partnerships, and unincorporated associations; and public unit accounts. Also called Account Category.

Brokered CD: A certificate of deposit account established at an insured bank by an agent or broker representing the deposits of one or multiple investors.

Certificate of Deposit (CD): A savings instrument that pays interest for a specified term, at a fixed or variable interest rate, and is redeemable at maturity. A CD is a type of deposit, not an account ownership category. The amount of coverage applicable to the CD holder depends on the ownership category (individual, joint, trust, IRA) in which the CD is held, and also on the other deposit accounts the holder has in that same category at the same bank. Also called Time Certificate and Investment Certificate.

Check: A form you complete that instructs your financial institution to withdraw the amount of money you specify on the check from your checking account and pay it to the person or organization named on the check.

Cashier's Check: A check drawn against a bank. It is considered a deposit and meets the requirements for deposit insurance coverage. Also called Official Instrument.

Interest Check: A check issued by a bank representing the interest earned on the account. Also called Official Instrument.

Printed Check: A document that tells your financial institution to pay a certain amount of money from your account to another person named on the document, called the payee or bearer.

Account Billing Cycle: The period between the end date of one statement and the start date of the next statement. The billing cycle is usually one month for credit cards, but its duration may vary.

Closing: When the ownership of the real estate is transferred from the seller to the buyer.

Bank Closure: Closure of a bank by its supervisory authority and appointment of the FDIC as receiver.

Sublease Clause: A section of a lease or rental agreement that indicates whether the property can be leased to another person by the tenant.

Pass-Through Coverage: Deposit insurance coverage provided for each participant's interest in an employee benefit plan. Pass-through coverage also applies when a trustee deposits funds on behalf of a client, provided certain requirements are met, such as registration and titling.

Coverage for Foreigners: Foreigners who are not U.S. citizens can have funds protected by FDIC insurance as long as the funds are deposited in an FDIC-insured institution and are within the insurance limits.

Credit Mix: Different types of credit accounts and loans that make up your credit history.

Holding Company: A company that owns or controls one or more banks. A technical definition, which is beyond the scope of this glossary, can be found in the "Bank Holding Company Act."

Treasury Offset: Occurs when all or part of your tax refunds or some other government payments are taken to pay the debt you owe to the federal government or state governments, including debts related to federal student loans and court-ordered child support.

Pledging Your Future Income: When you use the income you will receive in the future to make payments on debts you have incurred in the past.

Conditions: How you plan to use the money obtained in a loan, and the general economic conditions. Conditions depend on the type of loan, the economy, and how you plan to use the money. For example, a bank may be more cautious about approving new credit cards with high credit limits if unemployment rates are rising. In the context of a loan application, lenders may use conditions as a factor to determine your creditworthiness.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness: A program that forgives a portion of the federal student loan if the person is a full-time teacher and meets other requirements. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF): A federal program that forgives the remaining balance of certain federal student loans after you make 120 monthly payments while working full-time for a qualifying employer, such as certain nonprofit organizations or government agencies. There are also other requirements. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Credit Freeze: An action that prevents access to your credit reports. A credit freeze prevents new credit accounts from being opened and, in some states, prevents new accounts for other services, such as insurance and utilities, from being opened. Placing or lifting a freeze is free of charge. You have the legal right to freeze your credit reports.

Inquiry

Soft Inquiry: A type of inquiry to review your credit that does not affect your credit scores. This inquiry may occur when your information is provided by credit reporting agencies to companies so they can offer you credit, a job, or insurance.

Hard Inquiry: A type of inquiry to review your credit. An inquiry is created when a creditor or potential creditor reviews your credit file. A hard inquiry may have an effect on your credit scores. Examples of this type of inquiry are when your credit report was viewed in response to: Your credit card or loan application When you offered to be a co-signer on a loan

Contingencies: Statements in an offer to purchase a home that must be true; otherwise, the offer is void. A home inspection clause may be a contingency in a home purchase offer.

Lease or Rental Agreement: A contract between you and the property manager or owner.

Copayment: An insurance term that refers to the fixed dollar amount of each covered claim that the insured is responsible for paying. The insurance company pays the remaining balance according to the terms of the insurance policy. For example, if your insurance policy has a $50 copayment and the covered claim amount is $150, you would pay $50, and the insurance company would pay $100.

Corporation: An incorporated business that includes both for-profit and nonprofit entities. Corporation accounts constitute a separate category of ownership, along with a partnership or consortium and an unincorporated association, which are a separate ownership category.

Deposit Broker: A person or legal entity that acts as an intermediary in placing deposits in FDIC-insured banks.

Coinsurance: The percentage of each covered claim that the insured person is responsible for paying. The insurance company pays the remaining balance according to the terms of the insurance policy. For example, if your insurance policy has a coinsurance of 20%, that means you pay 20% of the cost of a covered claim, and the insurance company pays 80%.

Joint Credit: When you apply for a credit card or another loan with one or more people, based on the assets, income, repayment capacity, and credit history of all of you. All applicants are equally responsible for repaying the debt.

Available Credit: How much credit you have available to borrow. For example, on a credit card, available credit is calculated by subtracting your outstanding balance from your credit limit.

Individual Credit: When you apply for a credit card or another loan on your own, based on your assets, income, repayment capacity, and credit history. You are solely responsible for paying the credit card bill or loan payment.

Credit or Credit Profile: The ability to borrow money. It also refers to how you have paid your bills or debts in the past. Lenders may use the credit profile, sometimes called financial character, as a factor to determine your creditworthiness.

Revolving Credit: A form of credit that allows you to keep adding purchases to an outstanding balance as payments are made. A credit card is an example of revolving credit.

Time Deposit and Savings Account: A time deposit is an interest-bearing deposit account held at a financial institution or bank that has a specific maturity date. A savings account is a deposit account held at a bank or other financial institution that provides principal security and typically earns interest.

Joint Account: A deposit account under the ownership of two or more people, with equal rights to withdraw funds, and that does not designate beneficiaries. Joint accounts constitute a separate category of account ownership. All co-owners of a joint account must sign the deposit account signature card unless the account is a certificate of deposit (CD) or was established by an agent, designated person, guardian, custodian, executor, or conservator.

Agent Account: An account established by an individual or legal entity on behalf of the account holder—See also Trust Account, Power of Attorney, Brokered CD, and Attorney Trust Account.

Matched Savings Account: An account program, typically administered by local community-based organizations, that incentivizes saving money for a specific purpose. Organizations administering the program often match a portion or all of the deposits to the account.

Corporation, Partnership, or Unincorporated Association Account: A deposit account held in the name of a corporation, partnership, or unincorporated association engaged in independent activities. Corporation, partnership, or unincorporated association accounts constitute a separate category of account ownership. This category, however, does not include accounts held in the name of a sole proprietorship or sole proprietorship business, such as the personal deposits of the business owner.

Custodial Account: A trust account in which the custodian conducts account transactions on behalf of the account holder, usually a minor. Also called Uniform Transfer to Minors Act (UTMA) Account.

DDA (Demand Deposit Account): A checking account. DDA is a type of deposit, not an account ownership category. The amount of coverage available to the owner of a DDA depends on the ownership category (individual, joint, trust, IRA) in which the deposit account is held and other accounts the owner has in the same category at the same bank.

Money Market Deposit Account (MMDA): A savings account that allows the account holder to make a limited number of transactions per month. Since it is a deposit account, an MMDA is subject to FDIC insurance coverage. An MMDA is a type of deposit, not an account ownership category. The amount of FDIC insurance coverage applicable to the holder of an MMDA depends on the ownership category (individual, joint, trust, etc.) in which the account is held. These accounts are only available to individuals, nonprofit organizations, and government entities. It is different from a money market mutual fund, which is not insured by the federal government.

Money Market Deposit Account (MMDA): A deposit account at a federally insured financial institution that may offer a higher interest rate than a regular savings account. You may need to maintain more money in an MMDA account than you would for other accounts.

Escrow Account: A special account that collects funds from your monthly housing payments and reserves them to pay property taxes and insurance when due. When you obtain a loan to purchase a home (called a mortgage), your lender may require you to pay money as an escrow deposit for taxes and homeowners insurance, or you may have the option to do so.

Deceased Person's Account: An account held in the name of a deceased person or in the name of their estate. Also called Estate Account.

Attorney Trust Account (IOLTA): A trust account established by an attorney, which holds funds that the attorney maintains on behalf of one or more clients, and the accrued interest is paid to the State Bar Association or other legal assistance programs and organizations. Also called IOLTA Account.

Irrevocable Trust Account: A deposit account held in the name of a written trust in which the grantor (the person who created the trust) does not have the power to terminate or revoke the trust agreement, although the grantor may retain an interest in the trust assets. An irrevocable trust can be created upon the death of the grantor of a revocable trust, upon the execution or creation of an irrevocable trust agreement, or by law or court order. Irrevocable trust accounts constitute a separate category of account ownership. Due to the complexity of an irrevocable trust, you, your attorney, or your financial advisor should consult with the FDIC regarding deposit insurance coverage, as EDIE does not analyze irrevocable trusts.

Informal Revocable Trust Account: A deposit account held in the name of an informal trust created for estate planning in which the grantor retains control of the funds during their lifetime but also identifies beneficiaries who will receive the trust assets upon the grantor's death. Informal revocable trust accounts, which also include formal revocable trust accounts, constitute a separate category of account ownership. Also called POD, ITF Accounts.

Formal Revocable Trust Account: Deposits held in the name of a written trust created for estate planning. The grantor retains control of the funds during their lifetime but also identifies beneficiaries who will receive the trust assets upon the grantor's death. Also called Living Trust and Family Trust. Formal revocable trust accounts constitute a separate category of ownership, which also includes informal revocable trust accounts, payable-on-death accounts, "in trust for" accounts, testamentary accounts, or Totten trust accounts.

Government Account: An account established by an official custodian with funds from a public unit or political subdivision. Also called Public Unit Account. Government accounts constitute a separate category of account ownership.

Retirement Account: An account offered by an employer that helps provide financial security for when you are no longer working (retired). You choose to have money withheld from your paycheck and deposited into your retirement account. If your contributions are tax-deductible, the money you save on taxes means your take-home pay will not be reduced as much as the amount you contribute. Additionally, some companies offer to match a portion or all of the money you contribute to the plan. Federal law specifies that only the following types of retirement plan deposits qualify for coverage in the "certain retirement accounts" category:

Individual Retirement Account (IRA): An account that provides tax advantages for retirement savings. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) sets contribution and deduction limits. There are the following types of IRAs: traditional, Roth, SEP (Simplified Employee Pension) and SIMPLE (Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees). With a traditional IRA, contributions are usually tax-deductible. You do not pay taxes on the earnings of a traditional IRA until retirement, when withdrawals are taxed as income. With a Roth IRA, contributions are made with after-tax funds and are not deductible. However, earnings and withdrawals with a Roth IRA are tax-free.

IRA (Individual Retirement Account): Individual retirement account. A deposit account that conforms to Section 408(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Retirement accounts that meet these requirements are: traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs, SEP IRAs (Simplified Employee Pension), SIMPLE IRAs (Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees). All types of IRA deposit accounts are insured according to the "certain retirement accounts" category of account ownership.

Keogh Account: A deposit account held under a Keogh plan (also called an H.R. 10 plan), which is a retirement plan for business owners who are sole proprietors or partnerships. Self-directed Keogh plan deposit accounts are insured in the "certain retirement accounts" category, along with other accounts the holder has in that category. Keogh plan deposit accounts that are administered by a trustee for multiple participants are insured in the "employee benefit plan accounts" category.

ABLE Accounts: Tax-advantaged savings accounts for individuals with significant disabilities that manifested before age 26. ABLE accounts are designed to help individuals save for qualified disability expenses, including education costs. Offers and rules vary by the state in which you live and the program.

Employee Benefit Plan Accounts: Deposits held in any plan that meets the definition of employee benefit plans in section 3(3) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), including:

Defined contribution plans, such as a 401(k) plan, in which each participant has one or more accounts consisting of participant and/or employer contributions, and investments are directed by a plan administrator and not by each participant.

Defined benefit plans, in which the employer is required to pay an employee a benefit of a certain amount (e.g., an amount based on years of service and the retiree's salary at retirement).

Employee welfare or benefit plans, which are established by an employer or a labor union to provide employees with medical, hospitalization, or income benefits in case of illness, accident, or death. (Note: Welfare plans are generally funded through a trust.)

Keogh plans, as defined in section 401(k) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, and that are not self-directed. Employee benefit plan accounts constitute a separate category of account ownership.

Defined Contribution Plan Account: A deposit account held in the name of an employee benefit plan, as defined in section 3(34) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA). The most common types are classified under section 401(k) of the Act. Participants in such plans, and/or their employers, make regular contributions. These are generally made before taxes are deducted, as a way to save for retirement. A defined contribution plan can be established for an individual participant or multiple participants. When the plan participant(s) can direct the investment of their funds, including deposits in a specific FDIC-insured bank, the plan is considered "self-directed." Self-directed defined contribution plan accounts are insured under the "Certain Retirement Accounts" category of ownership. When a plan administrator (who may or may not be a plan participant) directs the plan's investments on behalf of all participants, the plan is NOT considered self-directed. Accounts held by these defined contribution plans are insured under the "Employee Benefit Plan Accounts" category of ownership.

Section 457 Plan Account: A deposit held in a deferred compensation plan for state employees. Deposits in section 457 plans for a person or state employee may receive coverage of up to $250,000 in the "certain retirement accounts" category, regardless of whether the specific plan is self-directed or not.

Mortgage Servicing Account: An account in which the mortgage servicer deposits payments from multiple borrowers. Each borrower's payments generally consist of the principal and interest (P&I) portion and the taxes and insurance (T&I) portion. The P&I portion of the account is insured up to $250,000 per borrower, separate from the deposits the borrower also has at the same bank. The T&I portion of each borrower, however, is added to the other individual ownership accounts the borrower has at the bank, and the aggregated amount is insured up to $250,000.

Estate Account: An account held in the name of a deceased person or in the name of their estate. Also called Deceased Account and is insured under the individual account category.

Public Unit Account: An account established by an official custodian that contains the funds of a public unit or political subdivision. Public unit accounts constitute a separate category of account ownership. Also called Government Account. The terms "public unit" and "political subdivision" include drainage, irrigation, navigation, improvement, levee, sanitary, power, and school districts, as well as bridge or port authorities and other special districts created by state law or agreements between states. The term "political subdivision" also encompasses any major subdivision or department of a public unit (state, county, or municipality) if the subdivision or department meets the following criteria: The creation of the subdivision or department has been expressly authorized by the laws of that public unit; Some governmental functions have been delegated to the subdivision or department by that law; and The subdivision or department is empowered to exercise exclusive control over funds for its exclusive use. The term "political subdivision" does not include subordinate or non-autonomous divisions, agencies, or boards within major subdivisions or departments. For assistance in determining whether a political subdivision meets the above requirements, contact the legal advisor of the political unit.

Trust Account: An account under the ownership of one party but held in a fiduciary capacity by another party. Fiduciary relationships may include, but are not limited to, an agent, trustee, guardian, executor, or custodian. Some common trust accounts are Uniform Transfer to Minors Act (UTMA) accounts, custodial accounts, IOLTA (attorney trust) accounts, and deposit accounts obtained through a broker.

Individual Account: An account in the name of a person without designated beneficiaries. Also called Simple Account.

Simple Account: An account in the name of an individual without designated beneficiaries. Simple accounts constitute a separate category of account ownership. Also called Individual Account.

NOW Account (Negotiable Order of Withdrawal): A negotiable order of withdrawal account. A deposit account in which the deposit institution has reserved the right to require written notice at least 7 days in advance before withdrawing or transferring funds from the account. These accounts are only available to individuals, nonprofit organizations, and government entities.

Testamentary Account: A revocable trust account in which the account title indicates that the deposits are payable to the designated or identified beneficiaries upon the account holder's death. See the definition for formal and informal trust accounts.

Annual Fee: When used in the context of a credit card, an annual fee is the money you must pay to the credit card provider each year for the card, whether you use it or not. Many credit cards do not have an annual fee. In some other types of loans, an annual fee may also be charged.

Official Custodian: An official custodian is an officer, employee, or agent of a public unit who has official custody of public funds and legally deposits the funds in an insured institution. To qualify as an official custodian, a person must have full authority—including control—over the funds. Control of public funds includes possession and authority to establish accounts in insured deposit institutions and to make deposits, withdrawals, and disbursements. For assistance in determining who is the official custodian of a public unit, contact the legal advisor of the public unit.

D

Initial Escrow Account Disclosure: Lists the costs the lender expects you to pay into a special account each month during the first year of your loan as part of a mortgage contract. This may include estimated taxes, insurance premiums, and other charges. The money in the special account (called an escrow account) is reserved to pay these expenses when due.

Credit Counseling Statement: A notice on a credit card statement explaining how to obtain information about credit counseling services.

Deductions: Money that is taken out of your gross pay to pay taxes, insurance premiums, union dues, retirement plan contributions, and other items. Deductions may be mandatory or voluntary.

Medicare Deduction: Taxes that are deducted from your salary under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA). Medicare contributions help pay for Medicare.

Social Security Deduction: Taxes that are deducted from your salary under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA). This deduction helps pay for old-age, survivor, and disability insurance. It may be called OASDI deduction.

Deductible: An insurance term that refers to the amount of money you agree to pay before an insurance company pays a claim. Depending on the type of insurance and the policy, you may have an annual deductible or a per-claim deductible, or possibly both. The annual deductible is the amount per year that you agree to pay before the insurance company pays its share. The per-claim deductible is the amount per covered claim that you agree to pay.

Annual Deductible: An insurance term that refers to the amount of money you must pay out of pocket each year before the insurance company begins to pay claims that year. It is common in health insurance.

Per-Claim Deductible: The amount you agree to pay for each covered loss; it is commonly used in auto insurance policies. If the covered loss exceeds the per-claim deductible, the insurance company will pay the rest according to the terms of the insurance contract.

Depreciation: A decrease in the value of an item over time.

Depositor: A person or entity (such as a corporation) that deposits funds in an FDIC-insured institution.

Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF): The deposit insurance fund. A fund maintained by the FDIC to insure deposits in closed financial institutions.

Deposit: Funds placed in an FDIC-insured bank that meet the requirements for FDIC insurance coverage (see Type of Deposit below).

Insured Deposits: Deposits in an FDIC-insured bank with balances equal to or less than the applicable FDIC insurance limits.

Direct Deposit: The automatic deposit of a portion or all of your salary, benefits, or other payments directly into the account you specify at a financial institution. Not all employers or benefit providers offer direct deposit.

Uninsured Deposit: The portion of a depositor's account(s) that exceeds the applicable FDIC insurance limit. Depositors with uninsured funds may recover some portion of this amount when the assets of the closed bank are liquidated.

Debt: Money owed to a person or company.

High-Cost Debt: Debt that is expensive, often the result of short-term loans with costly fees, high-interest rates, or both.

Debtor: Someone who owes money.

Closing Disclosures: Disclosures that list the final loan terms, final closing costs, and details of who pays and who receives money at closing. The lender must send you this document at least three business days before closing.

Automatic Debit: An electronic payment option that gives direct permission to a company, such as a merchant or lender, to withdraw payments from your account at a financial institution once or on a recurring basis.

E

EDIE - the FDIC's Electronic Deposit Insurance Estimator: allows the user to enter information about their deposit accounts at an insured bank and generates a report indicating which funds are insured and which funds are not (if any).

Garnishment: If you owe money, your creditors may take part of your income and assets directly to cover your debt, usually as a result of a court order.

Bank Account Garnishment: When money is taken from an account you have at a financial institution or in an investment to pay your debt. This occurs due to a court order.

Wage Garnishment: When your employer withholds a portion of your salary by court order to pay a debt you owe.

Default: When you are late on a certain number of loan payments, as determined by the lender or creditor.

Data Management Error: A type of error that can be found in credit reports. For example, when a credit report shows: Incorrect information that reappears after being corrected Accounts that appear multiple times with different creditors

Identity Error: A type of error that can be found in credit reports. For example, when a credit report shows: Incorrect identity information (wrong name, phone number, address) Accounts belonging to another person with the same or a similar name Incorrect accounts resulting from identity theft

Balance Error: A type of error that can be found in credit reports. For example, a credit report might include an account with an incorrect current balance.

Mixed File Error: A type of error that can be found in credit reports. The information of two consumers is mixed in the same credit report.

Social Media Scams: When criminals try to trick you into giving them your personal information on social media apps and sites, chat rooms, photo-sharing sites, and similar places. These scams sometimes start with a sales offer about an investment from someone you don't know.

Loan Estimate: A form you receive after applying for a mortgage. It provides important details about the loan you have applied for.

Exceptions or Exclusions: In the context of insurance, exceptions or exclusions are limits to the amount of insurance coverage or situations that the insurance will not cover.

F

Pay Date: The date you receive your net pay from your employer. There is often a delay between the end of the pay period and the pay date.

Payment Due Date: The date by which your creditor must receive your payment, which is different from the postmark date of your payment.

Trustee: A person authorized to conduct transactions on behalf of the trust. For irrevocable trusts, the trustee is usually someone other than the grantor.

Living Trust: A formal revocable trust created for estate planning. A living trust is one in which the grantor retains control of the funds during their lifetime but also identifies beneficiaries who will receive the trust assets upon the grantor's death. Formal revocable trust accounts constitute a separate category of account ownership, which also includes informal revocable trust accounts such as payable-on-death, in-trust-for, testamentary, or Totten trust accounts. Also called Family Trusts.

Family Trust: A formal trust created for estate planning. In a revocable family trust, the grantor retains control of the funds during their lifetime but also identifies beneficiaries who, upon the grantor's death, will receive the trust assets. Revocable trust accounts are a separate category of account ownership, which also includes informal revocable trust accounts such as payable-on-death, in-trust-for, testamentary, or Totten trust accounts. Also called Living Trusts.

Informal Revocable Trust: An informal revocable trust account—also called a payable-on-death, "in trust for," testamentary, or Totten trust account—is created when the account holder signs an agreement, usually part of the bank's signature card, stating that the funds will be payable to one or more beneficiaries upon the account holder's death. Revocable and irrevocable trusts are insured in the same category of account ownership.

Special Needs Trust: A trust designed to fund the long-term expenses and needs of a person with a disability. A special needs trust can be complex and generally requires an attorney for its establishment.

Pooled Special Needs Trust: A type of trust similar to a special needs trust. Instead of managing the assets of a single individual, the assets of several people with disabilities are pooled, which can reduce costs. A pooled trust is usually managed by a single entity or trustee, such as a nonprofit corporation, rather than an individual.

Grantor: A person who establishes a revocable or irrevocable trust. This person is also called the trust holder.

Co-Signing: The co-signer promises to pay the debt if the borrower does not pay it. The loan amount disbursed is given to the borrower and not to the co-signer.

IRS Form W-2: A form that an employer provides to employees, which includes the amount of money earned from the employer and the taxes withheld for the previous year.

IRS Form W-4: A form you complete and provide to your employer so they can withhold the correct amount of federal income taxes from your salary.

Bank Merger: When two institutions merge, or when one institution is absorbed by another.

G

Collateral: Something that has been pledged as security for the repayment of a loan. This only applies to secured loans. If the loan is not repaid, the lender may retain or take possession of what has been pledged as collateral. In the context of a loan application, lenders may use collateral as a factor to determine your creditworthiness.

Expenses: Ways to use your income: saving it, distributing it, and spending it.

Money Order: A paper document used to send money, including to pay bills. Money orders are prepaid, so they are only issued after the buyer pays the money for the order. They can generally be purchased at the United States Postal Service, banks, and other merchants.

H

Mortgage or Security Instrument: A document that gives a lender the right to take possession of certain property if the borrower does not repay the loan.

Conventional Mortgage: A loan for purchasing a home. This type of mortgage does not have special requirements for borrowers and is not guaranteed or insured by the government. Conventional mortgages are available to anyone, but they may be more difficult to be approved for some people than other types of mortgages.

Adjustable-Rate Mortgage: A mortgage loan in which the interest rate is adjusted according to a schedule, based on an index, or both. The details will be specified in the loan agreement.

Fixed-Rate Mortgage: A home loan in which the interest rate does not vary from the interest stated in the loan agreement.

I

Uncollectible: When a creditor gives up its attempts to collect a debt from you directly that has been in default. The creditor will likely assign or sell your debt to a debt collector. This means your debt has gone to collections and will appear on your credit reports in the collections section.

Default: Occurs when you do not repay a loan according to the terms of the loan agreement. For some loans, you may be in default as soon as you miss a payment. In others, many days, weeks, or months of non-payment may pass before the debt is considered in default.

Inflation: Inflation is the increase in the prices of goods and services over time. As prices rise, the purchasing power of a dollar decreases. Each dollar can buy a little less.

Payment Options Information: The ways in which the lender will allow you to make your payments. For example, you may be able to have the lender automatically deduct payments from a bank account so you don't have to remember to mail or deliver loan payments.

Personal Information: Information about you. For example, your name, address, and Social Security number.

Student Aid Report: A paper or electronic document you receive after submitting a FAFSA® application for federal student aid. It provides basic information about your eligibility for federal student aid and lists your answers to the FAFSA® questions. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Credit Report: A document that contains your credit history. There are multiple credit report producers, so you likely have more than one credit report.

Banking History Report: Reports that contain information about how a person has managed their bank accounts in the past. Financial institutions may use these reports to decide whether to allow someone to open an account. This report may also be called a checking account history report.

Income: Money a person receives from a job, a benefits program, a gift, or other sources.

Earned Income: Money you earn from your job, whether it's wages from a job, tips, contract work, or what you receive as a self-employed worker. Earned income also includes long-term disability benefits received before the minimum retirement age. Some examples of income that are not considered earned income are: interest and dividends, retirement income, Social Security, unemployment benefits, alimony, and child support.

Unpredictable Income: Income that varies in amount, timing, or both.

One-Time Income: Income you receive only once.

Regular Income: Income received on a set schedule.

Temporary Income: Income that may be predictable but only arrives at certain times of the year.

Home Inspection: When a qualified inspector conducts a thorough and unbiased examination of a home for a potential buyer to: Assess the physical condition: structure, construction, and mechanical systems. Identify items that need to be repaired or replaced. Estimate the remaining lifespan of major systems, equipment, structure, and finishes.

Home Inspector: In the context of home buying, a professional who identifies major issues with the home before you purchase it. May be called a house inspector.

Interest: Money a financial institution pays you for keeping money deposited with them. Interest is calculated based on the interest rate, the amount of money in your account, and how long the money remains in the account. Interest also refers to what a lender charges you for allowing you to use their money. It is expressed as a percentage and can be fixed or variable (adjustable).

Verifiable Interest: The portion of a participant in an employee benefit plan or trust that can be determined without contingencies.

Contingent Interest: The portion of a participant in a trust or employee benefit plan that cannot be determined due to uncertain conditions.

Non-Contingent Interest: The portion of a participant in a trust or employee benefit plan that can be determined without contingencies.

Compound Interest: Earning interest on the accumulated interest that is paid to you and remains in your account.

K

Emergency Kit: A collection of items, such as food, water, and medical supplies, that you would need to survive on your own for several days. It may also include cash. It can also be called a travel bag, go-bag, or BOB (by its acronym in English).

L

Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA): A federal law that requires taxes to be deducted from your salary. FICA taxes are for Social Security and Medicare.

Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA): A federal law that establishes federal standards that debt collectors must follow. This law prohibits debt collection companies from using abusive, unfair, or deceptive practices to collect debts.

Fair Housing Act (FHA): A federal law that protects people from discrimination in renting, buying, or financing a home based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, disability, or the presence of children (family status).

Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA): A federal law that grants you rights related to credit reports and other consumer reports.

Truth in Lending Act (TILA): A federal law that protects you against inaccurate and unfair billing and credit practices. It requires lenders to provide you with clear information about the cost of a loan so you can compare certain types of loans.

School Closure Discharge: A situation in which your federal student loans may be discharged, subject to specific requirements that must be met, if your school closes while you are enrolled or shortly after you leave. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Death Discharge: When the repayment of a federal student loan is no longer required because the borrower dies or the student for whom a parent took out a PLUS loan dies. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Debt Settlement: A financial arrangement you make with your creditor(s) to pay less money than you currently owe. You may have to pay income tax on the portion of the debt that was settled (that was not paid).

Coverage Limit: An insurance term that refers to the maximum amount of money an insurance company will pay for losses or events covered by the policy each year.

Credit Limit: How much money you can borrow from a creditor. Credit cards have credit limits, sometimes called credit lines.

Credit Line: How much money you can borrow from a creditor. Also called a credit limit.

Credit Line: A type of credit product that allows you to borrow money up to a certain amount called a credit line or credit limit. The balance of a credit line goes up when used and down when payments are made.

LLC (Limited Liability Company or Limited Liability Corporation): A business entity with characteristics of both corporations and partnerships. In the case of engaging in independent activity, a limited liability company receives separate deposit insurance coverage.

M

Medicaid: A joint federal and state program that helps with medical costs for some people with limited income and resources. Medicaid programs vary from state to state and may use a different name (for example, California's Medicaid program is called Medi-Cal).

Medicare: Medicare is a federal health insurance program for people aged 65 or older, certain younger people with disabilities, and people with end-stage renal disease (permanent kidney failure requiring dialysis or a transplant, sometimes called ESRD).

Reasonable Modification: A structural modification made to allow people with disabilities full enjoyment of housing and related facilities.

Amount Financed: The amount of credit that has been given to you or on your behalf. This is one of the terms used in a disclosure under the Truth in Lending Act (TILA).

Loan Amount: How much money a lender has lent or will lend you.

Balance Calculation Method: The way credit card providers calculate the interest owed on a credit card. There are several methods; the average daily balance method is the most popular.

Snowball Method: A method for reducing debt. You make extra payments on the debt with the lowest balance to pay it off first.

High-Cost Debt First Method: A method for reducing debt. You make extra payments on the debt that costs you the most to pay it off first.

Basic Insurance Amount (also known as the Standard Maximum Deposit Insurance Amount SMDIA): The basic FDIC insurance amount is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each account ownership category. Deposits held in different account ownership categories, such as individual accounts, joint accounts, trust accounts, and retirement accounts, are insured separately if the requirements for each ownership category are met, even if they are held at the same bank.

N

Sole Proprietorship: An unincorporated business in which all assets are owned by one person. Sole proprietors can use their own Social Security number or employer identification number. It is important to determine whether the account is a sole proprietorship or an incorporated business because incorporated businesses are insured in a separate category from individual accounts. Sole proprietorship accounts are insured in the individual account category, like the personal deposits of the owner. The expression DBA (doing business as) in the account title generally means that the account is a sole proprietorship.

Right to Cancel Notice: A notice you will receive if you refinance a mortgage under certain circumstances. The notice specifies that you can cancel the refinanced mortgage within three business days after closing. In the case of the initial purchase of a home, you do not have the right to cancel the loan once the closing documents are signed. Therefore, you will not receive this notice for the initial purchase of a home.

New Balance: In the context of credit cards, the amount of money you owe now. The new balance generally appears on the credit card statement.

Bank Routing Number: A nine-digit number that identifies the financial institution associated with a bank account. It is also called an ABA number or routing number. The bank routing number is generally found in the lower-left corner of a check, just before the bank account number. The bank routing number can also be found on bank and credit union statements, on their websites, and in mobile apps. A bank routing number is not the same as a bank account number.

O

SMART Goal: A goal that is specific, measurable, action-oriented, reachable, and time-bound.

Grantor: A person who establishes a revocable or irrevocable trust. This person is also called the trust holder or trustor.

P

Promissory Note: A document that contains the details of your loan, including: The amount of money you borrowed and must repay The interest rate of the mortgage loan The dates on which you must make loan payments The term or duration of the loan The total amount of money you will pay over the loan term If payment amounts can change and how Where you must send payments

Payable on Death (POD): A term used for revocable trust accounts to express the account holder's intention that the deposit account be payable to the designated beneficiaries upon the account holder's death. The terms (with their acronyms in English) that represent the same intention are "in trust for" (ITF) and "as trustee for" (ATF). POD, ITF, and ATF accounts are also called testamentary or Totten trust accounts. These accounts are insured in the revocable trust accounts category, along with formal revocable trust accounts.

Payments:

Automatic Bill Payment: A service that allows you to schedule and send payments electronically once or on a recurring payment schedule.

Person-to-Person (P2P) Payment: A type of payment initiated through a mobile app or other web-based service that transfers money from your account at a financial institution to another person or account.

Balloon Payment: A single, larger-than-usual payment at the end of a loan term.

Down Payment: A cash payment made when purchasing something on credit, such as a home or vehicle. The down payment reduces the amount of money that is financed.

Minimum Payment: The minimum amount of money you must pay for a debt in each billing cycle. Credit card statements indicate the minimum payment that must be made in the billing cycle.

Retained Interest: A retained interest is ANY circumstance in which the deposits held by the trust may be returned to, or used by, the grantor, or used by a trustee for the benefit of the grantor. The grantor must be alive for this condition to exist. For purposes of calculating insurance coverage, if the holder has retained an interest, EDIE assumes that the retained interest is 100% of the deposit balance.

Liability: Something you owe to others, usually money.

Net Worth: A measure of your financial stability or wealth calculated by subtracting your liabilities from your assets.

Named Perils: Hazards and disasters that an insurance policy will cover under the insurance contract.

Penalty APR: Refers to an increase in the interest rate on your credit card balance that the creditor applies if you do not pay your credit card bill on time. Review the documentation that accompanies the credit card to know if this charge can be applied and when.

Grace Period: Allows the borrower to delay payment for a short period of time. In the case of credit cards with a grace period, it is the time between the end of a billing cycle and the payment due date. In the case of federal student loans, it is the time between (1) when you leave school, take fewer credits than required by the loan, or the school closes, and (2) the date when you must start repaying the loan. The grace period for a federal student loan is usually about six months.

Pay Period: The period of work for which you are paid. It could be a week, two weeks, a month, or another period. For example, the pay period could be from December 1 to December 14.

Pharming (web traffic redirection): When criminals seek to obtain personal or private information by making fake websites appear legitimate.

Phishing: When criminals make phone calls or send text messages or emails to trick you into providing personal information that they can use to steal your identity. The calls, text messages, or emails appear to come (but do not) from a legitimate source, such as your bank, your utility company, a well-known merchant, your Internet service provider, or even a trusted government agency.

PITI: Acronym for the following words in English: Principal – The amount of money you borrow to buy a house Interest – Interest on the principal Taxes – Property or real estate taxes Insurance – Homeowners insurance premiums

Plans:

529 Plan: A tax-advantaged savings plan designed to help save money to pay for qualifying educational costs. Contributions to a 529 education savings plan go to an account managed by the plan's fund manager. Offers and rules vary by the state in which you live and the program.

Amortization Plan: A document you receive from the lender that tells you how much of each payment goes toward paying the principal and how much toward interest over the expected life of the loan.

Self-Directed Plan: This term means that participants in the particular retirement plan have the right to direct the investment of the assets held in their name by the plan. For deposit insurance purposes, the participant must be able to direct the funds to a specific FDIC-insured institution. The definition of "self-directed" relates to the FDIC insurance coverage requirement for certain retirement accounts.

Spending and Savings Plan: A tool that helps you compare your income and expenses, understand where your money goes, and make adjustments to how you use it to meet your goals. It may be called a budget.

Extended Payment Plan: A repayment plan for federal student loans in which payments are calculated over an extended period and may require fixed or gradually increasing payments. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Graduated Payment Plan: A repayment plan for federal student loans in which payments are calculated over a ten-year term. Payments start lower and usually increase every two years. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Pay As You Earn (PAYE) Plan: A repayment plan for federal student loans in which your payments are restructured based on your income. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Income-Based Repayment (IBR) Plan: A type of income-driven repayment plan for federal student loans. It sets your student loan monthly payment at an amount intended to be affordable based on your income and family size. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Income-Contingent Repayment (ICR) Plan: A type of income-driven repayment plan for federal student loans. It sets your student loan monthly payment at an amount intended to be affordable based on your income and family size. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Plan to Achieve Self-Support (PASS): A Social Security Administration program that allows people with disabilities to set aside money for items or services needed to achieve a specific educational or work goal. The money set aside is not counted when determining eligibility or benefits for certain programs.

Revised Pay As You Earn (REPAYE) Plan: A repayment plan for federal student loans in which your payments are restructured based on your income. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Certified Financial Planner (CFP): A professional who provides information on financial planning and investments, financial plans, and advice through commission or fee.

Loan Term: The duration of the loan, at the end of which it must be fully repaid.

Loan Term: A defined period of time you have to repay a loan.

Power of Attorney: A written statement that identifies a person as the attorney-in-fact of another with the powers specified in the document. A general power of attorney can be granted, or the authority can be limited to certain functions, such as deposits and withdrawals from a checking account. The statement must be executed in accordance with state laws and requirements.

Annual Percentage Yield (APY): In the case of interest-bearing accounts at financial institutions, the APY is the amount of interest you will earn annually, expressed as a percentage. The APY percentage is different from the interest rate because the APY also includes the effect of compound interest.

Prequalification: An informal way to get an estimate from a lender on the amount of money you can borrow.

Prepayment: Early repayment of all or part of a loan.

Lender: Qualifies you for a loan based on your creditworthiness and lends you money.

Insurance Premium: The amount of money you pay for an insurance policy.

Credit Products: Loans, credit cards, and other products offered by financial institutions.

Non-Deposit Investment Products: Investment products that include stocks, bonds, mutual funds, annuities, and Treasury investments (bonds, notes, and bills). Since they are not deposits, the FDIC does not insure these investments, even if purchased through a bank.

Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP): A federal program that provides nutritional benefits to low-income individuals and families who meet the requirements.

Loans:

Installment Loan: A type of loan in which a specific amount of money is borrowed at once and regular installment payments are made over a specified period.

Secured Loan: A loan with collateral. The lender can keep the collateral if the loan is not repaid according to the loan agreement. A mortgage is a secured loan.

Chattel Loan: A type of loan typically used to finance manufactured homes (mobile homes) located on rented land, that do not have permanent foundations, or both situations.

Joint Loan (being a co-borrower): Borrowing a loan jointly with one or more people. All co-borrowers are equally responsible for repaying the loan.

Debt Consolidation Loan: A new loan used to pay off some or all of the other debts one has.

Cooperative Loan: A loan to acquire a share in a cooperative.

Federal Housing Administration Loan (FHA Loan): A loan guaranteed by the Federal Housing Administration that may offer better terms than those available with a conventional loan.

Second Mortgage Loan: A loan taken out using the home as collateral while still having another loan secured by the same. It is sometimes used to provide financing to buy another home or to make necessary repairs.

Pawnshop Loan: A secured debt with the item you have pawned. If you do not make the payment when due, expect the pawnshop to keep your item and sell it.

Payday Loan or Payday Advance: A short-term, small-amount loan, often with a high-interest rate, in which you receive borrowed money immediately based on the expectation that you will repay the loan when you receive your next paycheck.

Private Student Loan: A non-federal loan to help pay for college and related educational expenses, funded by a bank, credit union, state agency, school, or another lender.

Federal Student Loan: A loan offered by the federal government to help pay for college, professional, vocational, or graduate education and related expenses. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Jumbo Loan: A mortgage for an amount that is above a certain money limit. A jumbo loan tends to be used for purchasing relatively expensive homes or in high-cost areas.

Unsecured Loan: A loan without collateral.

Revolving Loan: A type of loan in which you can borrow money up to a pre-approved credit limit. You can borrow, repay, and borrow again. Your payments vary based on the amount you owe and the interest rate. It is also called a revolving credit line or revolving credit.

Car or Vehicle Title Loan: Typically, a loan for a small amount of money and for a short time. To receive the loan, you give the lender the title to your vehicle (e.g., your car, truck, or motorcycle) as collateral. If you do not repay the loan as agreed, the lender can keep your collateral.

Government-Guaranteed Loans: Special government loans such as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans, U.S. Department of Agriculture loans, Veterans Administration (VA) loans, and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) loans. The federal government will guarantee a portion of these loans and reimburse the lender if the borrower does not pay.

Payment Deferment: Allows you to temporarily stop making payments or temporarily reduce your monthly loan payment for a specified period if you qualify. The requirements for deferred loan payments vary. For example, in the case of federal student loans, you may or may not be responsible for paying the interest that accrues during a deferment period. It depends on the type of federal student loan you have. More information at StudentAid.gov.

Credit Score: A number based on the information in your credit reports used to predict the likelihood that you will pay your bills and debts as agreed. There are multiple credit score producers, each with one or more scoring models. So you likely have more than one credit score.

Points: An upfront charge paid to a mortgage lender to reduce the interest rate on a mortgage.

Covered Loss: An insurance term that refers to the losses or events that are covered by an insurance policy.

R

Claim: An insurance term that refers to a notification to the insurance company that you have incurred a loss or experienced an event that you believe the insurance policy covers. Depending on the type of insurance and the policy, you may not have to file claims.

Rewards: Incentives you can earn based on your use of certain credit cards. Rewards may include cash back, points that can be used to purchase other goods and services, or airline miles that can be used to purchase airline tickets.

Transaction Register: A paper record used to note checks issued and deposits made into a checking account. Account Records; Bank Account Records; Deposit Account Records: Account records include signature cards, certificates of deposit (CDs), savings passbooks, ledgers, and computer records related to the bank's acceptance of deposits. Also called Bank Account Records and Deposit Account Records.

Rule of 72: A way to approximately calculate the time it will take for money to double in value, given a certain interest rate. Divide the number 72 by the interest rate (ignoring the percentage sign). For example, with an interest rate of nine percent, your money will double in value approximately every eight years (72 divided by 9 equals 8).

Insurance Regulations: The regulations governing the amount of insurance coverage provided by the FDIC to depositors of an insured depository institution. They can be found in 12 C.F.R. Part 330.

Debt-to-Income Ratio: A tool used by lenders to estimate whether someone can afford to borrow money. It calculates the percentage of a person's gross monthly income that goes toward debt payments. The ratio is calculated by dividing the total monthly debt payments by the gross monthly income. What is included in monthly debt payments and gross monthly income may vary by lender.

Gross Pay: The pay or salary before taxes and other deductions are subtracted (withheld).

Net Pay: Gross pay minus deductions, such as Social Security and income tax withholdings. It is the payment you receive.

Risk: The potential for harm. Harm includes losing something of value or its value decreasing.

Identity Theft: A crime that occurs when someone uses a person's identifying information without authority to do so.

S

Previous Balance: The money you owed as shown on your last bill.

Account Balance: The dollar amount, including principal and interest, of a specific account.

Supplemental Security Income (SSI): Benefits that the federal government pays to eligible disabled adults and children based on financial need.

Insurance:

Renter's Insurance: A type of insurance policy that helps renters recover financially from losses or damage to their personal possessions due to a hazard or disaster specifically named in the insurance policy. It also provides coverage in case someone is injured in the rented home. Renter's insurance does not cover the physical building.

Deposit Insurance: Insurance coverage provided by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) for deposit products in insured banks and by the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) for deposit products in insured credit unions. In the event of a failure of an insured institution, people with deposit products in the failed entity are guaranteed to receive the principal and accrued interest on their deposit products, up to $250,000 per ownership category. For example, if a person had a total of deposits in an institution that included a savings account solely in their name with a principal balance of $195,000 and $3,000 of accrued interest, the full amount of $198,000 would be insured. This is because the principal plus interest does not exceed the $250,000 insurance limit for single ownership accounts.

Disability Insurance: An insurance product that protects you from financial hardship when a covered illness or injury prevents you from earning a living.

Life Insurance: An insurance policy that pays money after your death. It may also have other benefits.

Homeowners Insurance: Insures your home and personal belongings against damage or loss. It also insures you in case someone is injured while on your property. It generally does not cover damage caused by floods or earthquakes and may not cover expensive items. However, you may be able to add separate coverage for those events and items.

Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI): A type of insurance that protects the lender, not you, if you stop paying your loan. The lender may require PMI insurance when the down payment is less than 20 percent of the purchase price or home value.

Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI): Benefits that the federal government pays to people with disabilities (and certain family members) if they are insured, meaning they have worked and paid Social Security taxes long enough to qualify for this benefit.

Skimming: When criminals steal credit or debit card numbers with a special storage device. The device is hidden in ATMs and point-of-sale terminals (where you swipe the card at retail locations, such as gas stations). You swipe your card, and they get the card number, which they try to use to purchase goods or services.

Smishing: When scammers send deceptive text messages to trick consumers into providing personal information that the scammers will use to commit fraud.

Overdraft: Occurs when a transaction is made on an account even though there is not enough money in the account at a financial institution to cover it.

Partnership or Consortium: An association of two or more people or entities formed to carry out, as co-owners, an unincorporated business. Partnership accounts, along with corporation or unincorporated association accounts, constitute a separate category of account ownership.

Credit Card Applicant: A person who applies for a credit card.

Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA): An application used to determine eligibility for various types of federal student aid, such as loans, work-study programs, and grants. Learn more at StudentAid.gov or the myStudentAid mobile app.

Spear Phishing: When criminals target groups of people who have something in common in an attempt to get them to reveal confidential information.

Grant: Money given to someone for a specific purpose and often called "gift aid" because it usually does not have to be repaid. Grants are often need-based. The federal government has several grant programs that can help pay for education expenses. More information at StudentAid.gov.

T

Cards:

ATM Card: A card that can be used at ATMs to conduct transactions on an account. You may also be able to make some purchases with an ATM card.

Charge Card: A card that allows you to make purchases and requires you to pay the entire balance each month. Unlike a credit card, you do not have the option to carry over part of the balance to another month.

Credit Card: A type of revolving credit line. The balance of a credit card goes up when used to make purchases and down when payments are made.
